title: USB-C
wiki_lead:
USB‑C, or USB Type‑C, is a 24-pin reversible connector (not a protocol) that supersedes all previous USB connectors, which were designated legacy in 2014. This connector also supersedes Mini DisplayPort and Lightning connectors. USB-C is widely used for multiple purposes: exchanging data with peripheral devices, such as external drives, mobile phones, keyboards, trackpads, and mice, and between hosts; transferring A/V data to displays and speakers; and powering peripheral devices and being powered by power adapters, either through directly wired connectors or indirectly via hubs and docking stations. This connector type can be used for other data transfer protocols besides USB, such as Thunderbolt, PCIe, DisplayPort, and HDMI. It is extensible, allowing the support of future protocols.
The design for the USB‑C connector was initially developed in 2012 by members of the USB Implementers Forum, with Intel, HP Inc., and Texas Instruments being distinguished on the design document, though Apple Inc. and Microsoft, among others, also contributed. The Type‑C Specification 1.0 was published by the USB Implementers Forum (USB-IF) on August 11, 2014. In 2016 it was adopted by the International Electrotechnical Commission as IEC 62680-1-3.
The USB Type‑C connector has 24 pins and is reversible. The designation C distinguishes it from the various USB connectors it replaced, all termed Type‑A, Type‑B, or, for receptacles only, Type‑AB. Whereas every earlier valid USB cable had a host end A and a peripheral device end B, a USB‑C cable connects either way (and the devices handle the logical A–B distinction). For interoperation with older equipment, there are Type-C-to-legacy cables; such a cable has a Type‑C plug at one end and either a Type‑A (host) or a Type‑B (peripheral device) plug at the other.
The designation C (Type-C or USB-C) refers only to the connector's physical configuration, or form factor, not to be confused with a cable or port's specific capabilities and performance, such as Thunderbolt 3, DisplayPort 2.0, or USB 3.2 Gen 2×2. While USB‑C is the single modern connector for all USB protocols, there are valid uses of the connector that do not involve any USB protocol. Depending on the protocols supported by all connected devices – host, intermediate devices (hubs), and peripheral devices – a USB‑C connection can provide much higher data rates and electrical power than anything using the superseded connectors.
A device with a Type‑C connector does not necessarily implement any USB transfer protocol, USB Power Delivery, or any of the Alternate Modes: the Type‑C connector is common to several technologies while mandating only a few of them.
USB 3.2, released in September 2017, fully replaced the USB 3.1 (and therefore also USB 3.0) specifications. It preserves the former USB 3.1 SuperSpeed and SuperSpeedPlus architectures and protocols, with transfer rates of 5 and 10 Gbit/s, and introduces two two-lane operational modes with the same signalling rates in each lane, doubling the transfer rates to 10 and 20 Gbit/s. These are only applicable with Full-Featured USB‑C cables and hosts, hubs, and peripheral devices that use them.

The USB4 specification, released in 2019, is the first USB protocol standard that is applicable exclusively via USB‑C.

These are only applicable with Full-Featured USB‑C cables and hosts, hubs, and peripheral devices that use them.

The USB4 specification, released in 2019, is the first USB protocol standard that is applicable exclusively via USB‑C.


Ease of use
The USB‑C standard simplifies usage by specifying cables having identical plugs on both ends; orientation is moot. Also, the plugs are flat but can be inserted in either orientation.


Symmetry
Mechanically, USB‑C receptacles have two-fold rotational symmetry – a plug may be inserted into a receptacle in either of two orientations.
Electrically, USB‑C plugs are not symmetrical, as can be seen in the tables of pin layouts. Also, some contacts are wired straight through and some are crossed over, as shown in the table of cable wiring.
Though a Type‑C–Type‑C cable is symmetrical, the connected devices still have logical host (A) and peripheral device (B) roles. If both devices are only capable of the same role, no damage occurs but no link is established; if both devices are capable of both roles, they negotiate to determine which takes which role. Determination of this host-to-peripheral-device relationship is accomplished through a Configuration Channel (CC) that is connected through the cable.


Universal application
The USB‑C standard attempts to eliminate the need to have different cables for other communication technologies, such as Thunderbolt, PCIe, HDMI, DisplayPort and more. Since the introduction in 2014, many companies have adopted the USB‑C standard into their products. USB‑C cables can contain circuit boards and processors, giving them much more capability than simple circuit connections.


Overview
USB‑C cables interconnect hosts and peripheral devices, replacing various other electrical cables and connectors, including all earlier (legacy) USB connectors, HDMI connectors, DisplayPort connectors, and 3.5 mm audio jacks.
USB Type‑C and USB‑C are trademarks of the USB Implementers Forum, Inc.

The 24-pin double-sided connector is slightly larger than the non-SuperSpeed, USB 2.0 Micro connectors, with a USB‑C receptacle opening measuring 8.34 mm × 2.56 mm, 6.20 mm deep.


Cables
Type‑C cables can be split among various categories and subcategories. The first one is USB 2.0 vs Full-Featured. USB 2.0 Type‑C cables have very limited wires and are only good for USB 1 and USB 2 communications and Power Delivery. They are also called charging cables colloquially. Conversely, Full-Featured cables need to have all wires populated and in general support Alternate Modes, and they are further distinguished by their speed ratings.
Full-Featured cables exist in different speed grades. Their technical names, the operation modes, use the Gen x notation, each higher number expressing increasing capabilities in terms of data rate. The marketing names are based on the nominal data rates: "USB 5Gbps", "USB 10Gbps", "USB 20Gbps", "USB 40Gbps", and so on. Full-Featured cables can support at least USB 3.x, USB Power Delivery and DisplayPort.
A Gen 1 (signalling rate of 5 Gbit/s) cable supports the Gen 1 rate on each of its two lanes (2 × 2 twisted data wire pairs). It can be used to establish a USB 3.2 Gen 1×2 operation mode with nominally 10 Gbit/s (2 × 5 Gbit/s) between two devices capable of USB 3.2 or later connected with a Full-Featured USB-C cable. 
According to the USB4 1.0 and 2.0 specifications, implementation of the USB 3.2 Gen 2×2 operation mode, resulting in nominally 20 Gbit/s, is optional; indeed most USB4 controllers do not implement it. In other words, the "USB 20Gbps" will only be achieved by a USB4 or more modern version of an operation mode, such as USB4 Gen 2×2, with USB4-capable devices and Full-Featured USB-C cables (and intermediate hubs) of a rate of "USB 20Gbps" (i.e. all four twisted data-wire pairs are wired) or higher between a host and a peripheral device.
The USB Implementers Forum certifies valid cables so they can be marked accordingly with the official logos and users can distinguish them from non-compliant products. There have been simplifications in the logos. Previous logos and names also referenced specific USB protocols like SuperSpeed for the USB 3 family of connections or USB4 directly. The current official names and logos have removed those references as most full-featured cables can be used for USB4 connections as well as USB 3 connections.
In order to achieve greater cable lengths, cable variants with active electronics to amplify the signals also exist. The Type‑C standard mostly mandates that these active cables behave similarly to passive cables with vast backwards compatibility, but they are not required to support all possible features and typically have no forward compatibility to future standards. Optical cables are even allowed to further reduce the backwards compatibility. For example, an active cable may not be able to use all high-speed wire pairs in the same direction (as used for DisplayPort connections) but only in the symmetric combinations expected by classic USB connections. Passive cables have no such limitations.


Power Delivery

Every USB‑C cable must support at least three amps of current and up to 20 volts, for up to 60 watts of power, according to the USB Power Delivery (PD) specification. Cables were also allowed to support up to 5 A while retaining the 20 V limit, allowing up to 100 W of power; however, the 20 V limit for 5 A cables has been deprecated in favor of 48 V. The combination of 48 V support and 5 A current support is called Extended Power Range (EPR) and allows for up to 240 W (48 V × 5 A) of power according to the USB PD specification.


eMarker
Each Type‑C cable except the most basic, supporting only up to USB 2.0 and 60 W (20 V × 3 A), must contain electronics, called an eMarker in the standard, that identify the cable and its capabilities via the Configuration Channel (CC). This identification data includes information about product and vendor, cable connectors, supported USB signalling protocols (USB 2.0, USB 3.x, etc), passive vs active construction, use of VCONN power, available VBUS voltages and currents, latency, transmit vs receive directionality, SOP controller mode, and hardware and firmware versions. It also can include further vendor-defined messages (VDM) that detail support for Alternate Modes or vendor-specific functionality outside of the USB standards.


Hosts and peripheral devices
For any two pieces of equipment connecting over USB, one is a host (with a downstream-facing port, DFP) and the other is a peripheral device (with an upstream-facing port, UFP). Some products, such as some mobile phones, can take either role, whichever is opposite that of the connected equipment. Such equipment is said to have Dual-Role-Data (DRD) capability, which was known as USB On-The-Go in earlier specifications. With USB‑C, when two such devices are connected, the roles are first randomly assigned, but a swap can be commanded from either end, although there are optional path and role detection methods that would allow equipment to select a preference for a specific role. Furthermore, Dual-Role equipment that implements USB Power Delivery may swap data and power roles independently using the Data Role Swap and Power Role Swap processes. This allows for charge-through hub and docking station applications such as a portable computer acting as a host to connect to peripherals but being powered by the dock, or a computer being powered by a display, through a single USB‑C cable.
USB‑C devices may optionally provide or consume bus power currents of 1.5 A and 3.0 A (at 5 V) in addition to baseline bus power provision; power sources can either advertise increased USB current through the configuration channel or implement the full USB Power Delivery specification using both the BMC-coded configuration line and the legacy BFSK-coded VBUS line.
All USB connectors aside from Type-C (that is, all 23 Standard, Mini, and Micro connectors, or, equivalently, all 23 Type‑A, Type‑B, and Type‑AB connectors) are designated legacy. Connecting legacy and modern, USB‑C equipment requires either a legacy cable assembly (a cable with either Standard‑A plug or any Type‑B plug at one end and a Type‑C plug at the other) or, in very specific cases, a legacy adapter assembly.
An older device can connect to a modern (USB‑C) host by using a legacy cable with a Type-C plug on the host (A) end and any Type-B plug (Standard-B, Mini-B, or Micro-B) on the peripheral (B) end. Similarly, a modern peripheral device can connect to a legacy host by using a legacy cable with a USB‑C plug on the peripheral device (B) end and a (USB 2 or USB 3) Standard-A plug on the host (A) end. Legacy adapters with USB‑C receptacles are "not defined or allowed" by the specification because they can create "many invalid and potentially unsafe" cable combinations (being generally any cable assembly with two A ends
grok_lead: USB Type-C, commonly abbreviated as USB-C, is a standardized 24-pin reversible connector for Universal Serial Bus (USB) interfaces, enabling simultaneous transmission of power, data, and video signals through a single, symmetrical port design. Developed by the USB Implementers Forum (USB-IF), the specification was released in August 2014 to address the need for a robust, user-friendly connector suitable for compact devices like smartphones, laptops, and tablets. Key capabilities include data transfer rates up to 40 Gbps via USB4, power delivery up to 240 W with USB Power Delivery 3.1, and support for alternate modes such as DisplayPort for video output. USB-C's widespread adoption marks a significant achievement in standardizing connectivity, reducing the proliferation of proprietary cables and ports, though implementations vary in supported speeds and features, leading to persistent compatibility issues. Regulatory efforts, exemplified by the European Union's mandate effective December 28, 2024, requiring USB-C for most new portable electronic devices to curb e-waste, have accelerated its dominance but ignited debates over whether such enforced uniformity hampers innovation in faster-charging or higher-performance alternatives.
